title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: from Scripture authority — affirmative and negative
latin: Tertio argumentamur ab auctoritate Scripturarum, tam affirmative quam negative, hoc modo. Scripturae Dei εὐδοκίαν sive beneplacitum causam praedestinationis nostrae passim commemorant; fidem autem praevisam nunquam sive causam, sive conditionem, sive antecedaneum praedestinationis statuunt. Ergo non oportet nos a puro beneplacito Dei ad fidem praevisam hoc ineffabile praedestinationis beneficium transferre. Huc faciunt illa Scripturae loca, Rom. ix. 11, Cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, ut propositum Dei secundum electionem maneret; et Ephes. i. 11, In quo electi sumus, cum essemus praedestinati secundum propositum; et alia consimilia.
pass_a: Thirdly we argue from the authority of the Scriptures, both affirmatively and negatively, in this way. The Scriptures of God everywhere commemorate God's εὐδοκία or good pleasure as the cause of our predestination; but they never set down foresighted faith as either the cause, or the condition, or the antecedent of predestination. Therefore we ought not to transfer this ineffable benefit of predestination from the pure good pleasure of God to foresighted faith. Hither tend those places of Scripture, Rom. 9:11, When they had done nothing good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand; and Eph. 1:11, In whom we were chosen, being predestinated according to purpose; and others like them.
pass_b: Third argument: from the authority of Scripture, both yes and no. Scripture everywhere names God's εὐδοκία — his good pleasure — as the cause of our predestination; it never sets foresighted faith down as cause, condition, or antecedent. So we must not shift this ineffable benefit off pure good pleasure onto foresighted faith. So Rom. 9:11 (when they had done nothing good or evil, that God's purpose according to election might stand) and Eph. 1:11 (chosen in him, predestined according to purpose) — and the like.

good pleasure as cause of predestination

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: no Scripture tip for election from foresight faith — Si credideris, praedestinaberis?
latin: Jam e contra, adversarii ne unum quidem apicem ex Scripturis proferre possunt quo innuatur homines fuisse electos prae aliis ex praevisa antecedentis fidei in illis conditione. At si decretum praedestinandi praerequirat conditionem credendi, atque hac conditione impleta electio credentis consequatur, stipulatio haec ex sacris Scripturis est demonstranda. Nam fingere promissiones aut pacta extra verbum Dei est summae temeritatis. Quaero igitur, Ubi habetur haec promissio, Si credideris, praedestinaberis? Vel, Quicunque crediderint, praedestinabuntur? Extat promissio talis, Quisquis crediderit, salvabitur; quia Deus exigit conditionem fidei tanquam antecedaneum ad salutem decretam: At non extat haec, Quisquis crediderit, aut quisquis praevidetur crediturus, praedestinabitur; quia Deus non exigit fidem tanquam antecedaneum ad suum decretum.
pass_a: Now on the contrary, the adversaries cannot produce even one tip from the Scriptures by which it is hinted that men were elected before others from the foresighted condition of antecedent faith in them. But if the decree of predestining presupposes the condition of believing, and the election of the believer follows upon that condition fulfilled, this stipulation must be demonstrated from the sacred Scriptures. For to invent promises or covenants outside the word of God is the height of temerity. I ask therefore, Where is this promise found, If you shall have believed, you shall be predestined? Or, Whosoever shall have believed shall be predestined? There exists such a promise, Whosoever shall have believed shall be saved; because God requires the condition of faith as antecedent to decreed salvation: But there does not exist this, Whosoever shall have believed, or whosoever is foreseen as about to believe, shall be predestined; because God does not require faith as antecedent to his decree.
pass_b: On the other side, adversaries cannot produce so much as one tip of Scripture hinting that men were chosen above others from a foresighted condition of prior faith. If the predestining decree really presupposes believing, and election follows once that condition is met, that bargain must be shown from Holy Scripture — inventing promises outside God's word is sheer temerity. Where then is If you believe, you shall be predestined? Or Whoever believes shall be predestined? There is Whoever believes shall be saved — God requires faith as antecedent to decreed salvation. There is no Whoever believes (or is foreseen to believe) shall be predestined — God does not require faith as antecedent to his decree.

lemmas.gloss: not even one tip from Scripture

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: Hague reply — foresight faith not cause; Davenant — word-catching and merit
latin: Sed respondentes Colloquutores Hagienses; Primo, se nunquam ponere praevisam fidem esse causam electionis, ac proinde non contravenire Scripturis, quae statuunt Dei εὐδοκίαν, vel solum beneplacitum esse ejus causam. Imo totidem verbis profitentur, causam, cur Deus singularem aliquam personam elegerit ad salutem, non esse fidem ejus, sed solum beneplacitum, gratiam, imo meram gratiam Dei. Sed haec omnia sunt mera verborum aucupia. Nam qui ponunt actum fidei perseverantis esse conditionem a Deo requisitam, ad cujus intuitum semper eligit, et ob cujus absentiam semper praeterit, ii vim causalem fidei adscribunt, imo meritoriam, eo sensu quo meriti vocabulum ab Augustino reliquisque Theologis in disceptationibus contra Pelagianos usurpatur. Sic Augustinus, Quis dicat illum qui jam coepit credere, ab illo in quem credidit nihil mereri?
pass_a: But the Hague Colloquy respondents reply; First, that they never set down foresighted faith as the cause of election, and therefore do not contravene the Scriptures, which establish God's εὐδοκία, or good pleasure alone, as its cause. Indeed in so many words they profess that the cause why God elected any particular person to salvation is not that person's faith, but only good pleasure, grace, yea the mere grace of God. But all these things are mere word-catching. For those who set down the act of persevering faith as a condition required by God, at the intuition of which he always elects, and for whose absence he always passes by, ascribe to faith a causal force, yea a meritorious one, in that sense in which the word merit is used by Augustine and the rest of the theologians in disputes against the Pelagians. So Augustine, Who would say that he who has already begun to believe merits nothing from him in whom he has believed?
pass_b: The Hague Colloquy speakers answer first: they never call foresighted faith the cause of election, so they do not fight Scripture naming εὐδοκία — good pleasure alone — as cause. They even say outright that why God elects any one person to salvation is not that person's faith, but only good pleasure, grace, mere grace. Word-catching, all of it. Whoever makes persevering faith the condition God requires — at whose sight he always elects, and for whose absence he always passes by — gives faith causal force, even meritorious force, in Augustine's anti-Pelagian sense of merit. So Augustine: who would say that one who has already begun to believe merits nothing from him in whom he believed?

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: Prosper, Hilary, Faustus — election-on-faith always meant prior merit
latin: Nec Augustinus solummodo arguit beneficium illud ex merito dari, quod datur ex fidei conditione praeeunte, sed (quod notatu dignum est) quicunque olim electionem ad vitam ex conditione fidei suspenderunt, inde dignitatem et meritum antecedaneum in electis agnoverunt. Sic Prosper in Epist. ad Augustinum, ubi exponit sententiam illorum qui reliquiae Pelagianorum appellabantur: Quantum ad Deum pertinet, omnibus paratam vitam aeternam esse dicunt; quantum autem ad arbitrii libertatem, ab his eam apprehendi qui Deo sponte crediderint, et auxilium gratiae merito credulitatis acceperint. Sic etiam Hilarius ad Augustinum scribens de eadem materia, ostendit eos qui rejiciebant electionem secundum Dei propositum, et introducebant electionem secundum fidei et paenitentiae praevisionem, in hac fide et conversione meritum et causam electionis agnovisse: Eo merito quo voluerint et crediderint a suo morbo se posse sanari, etc. Et Paulo post, Si qualiscunque dolor oriatur, hanc ipsam dicunt causam propter quam alius assumatur, alius rejiciatur. Denique Faustus Regiensis, qui accuratissime Semipelagianorum sententiam tutatur, sicut electionem ex fide praevisa statuit, ita etiam ex merito eandem fieri non dissimulat: Praescientia, inquit, gerenda praenoscit, postmodum praedestinatio retribuenda describit; illa praevidet merita, haec praeordinat praemia. Nimis igitur arguti sunt, et a majoribus suis desciscunt Remonstrantes, quando ponunt Deum eligere homines secundum praescientiam fidei, et tamen negant fidem praevisam esse causam dictae electionis.
pass_a: Nor does Augustine alone argue that that benefit is given from merit which is given from a preceding condition of faith, but (what is worthy of note) whoever of old suspended election to life upon the condition of faith thereby acknowledged an antecedent dignity and merit in the elect. So Prosper in the Letter to Augustine, where he expounds the opinion of those who were called the remnants of the Pelagians: As far as concerns God, they say eternal life is prepared for all; but as far as concerns free choice, it is apprehended by those who have spontaneously believed God, and have received the help of grace by the merit of believing. So also Hilary writing to Augustine on the same matter shows that those who rejected election according to God's purpose, and introduced election according to foresight of faith and penitence, acknowledged in this faith and conversion the merit and cause of election: By that merit by which they have willed and believed they can be healed of their disease, etc. And a little later, If any grief whatsoever arises, they say this very thing is the cause on account of which one is taken and another rejected. Finally Faustus of Riez, who most carefully defends the Semi-Pelagian opinion, as he establishes election from foresighted faith, so also does not dissemble that the same is done from merit: Foreknowledge, he says, knows beforehand what is to be done; afterwards predestination describes what is to be retributed; the one foresees merits, the other preordains rewards. Too subtle therefore are the Remonstrants, and they desert their elders, when they set down that God elects men according to foresight of faith, and yet deny that foresighted faith is the cause of said election.
pass_b: Augustine is not alone: whoever of old hung election to life on a faith-condition thereby admitted prior dignity and merit in the elect. Prosper (Letter to Augustine), on the so-called Pelagian remnants: as far as God goes, eternal life is prepared for all; as far as free choice goes, it is grasped by those who spontaneously believed, and received grace help by the merit of believing. Hilary to Augustine: those who rejected election according to God's purpose and brought in election by foresight of faith and penitence recognized in that faith and conversion the merit and cause of election — by the merit of willing and believing they can be healed, and later, whatever grief arises, they call that the very cause why one is taken and another rejected. Faustus of Riez, careful Semi-Pelagian: as he grounds election in foresighted faith, so he does not hide that it is also from merit — Foreknowledge knows what will be done; predestination then describes the retribution; the one foresees merits, the other preordains rewards. Remonstrants are too clever, and desert their elders, when they have God elect by foresight of faith and still deny that foresighted faith is the cause.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3: second Hague reply — God regards faith as medium to life, not condition of election
latin: Secundo respondent, Etiamsi totidem verbis in Scripturis non reperiatur, Deum nos elegisse cum conditione si in illum credamus, ex eo tamen non posse concludi, Deum in electione non respexisse ad fidem. At regerimus, non modo totidem verbis, sed nullis aequipollentibus, nullis unde id recte deduci potest, hoc exprimi in Scriptura. Neque tamen negamus omnem respectum aut conditionem fidei in Deo eligente. Respicit enim et considerat fidem a se electis ingenerandam, tanquam medium quo pervenitur ad vitam: non respicit tanquam conditionem ab hominibus antecedenter praestitam aut praestandam, qua mediante pervenitur ad ipsam electionem.
pass_a: Secondly they reply, Even if it is not found in so many words in the Scriptures that God elected us with the condition if we believe in him, yet from that it cannot be concluded that God in electing did not have respect to faith. But we rejoin, not only is this not expressed in Scripture in so many words, but not by any equivalent words, nor by any from which it can rightly be deduced. Nor yet do we deny every respect or condition of faith in God electing. For he regards and considers the faith to be ingenerated by himself in the elect, as the medium by which one arrives at life: he does not regard it as a condition antecedently performed or to be performed by men, by means of which one arrives at election itself.
pass_b: Second reply: even if Scripture nowhere says in so many words that God elected us on condition we believe, you still cannot conclude he had no regard to faith in electing. We answer: not only is it missing totidem verbis — there are no equivalent words, nothing from which it can rightly be drawn. We do not deny every regard to faith in electing God. He regards the faith he will ingenerate in the elect as the medium by which one reaches life — not as a condition men have already performed or must perform in order to reach election itself.

lemmas.gloss: not in so many words, nor equivalents
faith as medium to life, not to election

title: Cap. VI Arg. 3 close: good pleasure vs foresight faith — Rom. 4:16 not parallel for election
latin: Postremo dicunt Remonstrantes, nos errare, quando beneplacitum sive meram Dei gratiam et fidem praevisam in hoc negotio praedestinationis opponimus; quasi essent dicamus ex mera gratia et beneplacito, atque ex praevisa fide eligere; cum Apostolus ex eo quod haereditas sit ex fide, concludat eam esse ex gratia, Rom. iv. 16. Sed non est par ratio praedestinationis sive electionis obtinendae, et haereditatis regni caelestis adeundae. In negotio electionis esse ex fide, et esse ex mera gratia sunt ἐναντία, quia haec fides praesupponitur electioni, quae est ad primam gratiam, et scaturigo omnis gratiae salutiferae. At in causa adeundae vitae aeternae non sunt ἐναντία, quia haec fides est purae gratiae donum; et sic vitae praemium quod credenti redditur, est gratia pro gratia. Huc accedit, quod cum Deus humano generi proposuerit duplicem viam consequendae salutis, unam per opera Legis, Hoc fac, et vives; aliam per fidem Mediatoris, Crede, et salvus eris, recte dicitur ex gratia dari, quod datur ex fide; sicut ex operibus, quod datur ex Lege. Fuit enim gratiae Evangelicae singulare beneficium, relaxato foedere legali, salvare peccatores per fidem. At vero ex altera parte nunquam probabunt Remonstrantes Deum ordinasse duplicem modum praedestinandi homines: unum secundum opera, et alium secundum fidem. Si ergo quidam homines ex actu credendi ab illis praestito eligerentur, alii ob eundem actum omissum non eligerentur, discrimen hoc oriretur non ex speciali aliquo pacto aut actu gratiae Divinae, sed ex discriminatis actibus voluntatum humanarum. Esset enim praedestinatio Petri non ex speciali gratia Dei, sed ex speciali opere Petri: quia credere hic consideratur ut opus arbitrii per gratiam praeventi, oppositum contrario actui discredendi; non ut opus pacti alicujus Evangelici, oppositum pacto Legali, cum de praedestinatione talia pacta non exstent in utramvis partem.
pass_a: Lastly the Remonstrants say that we err when we oppose good pleasure or the mere grace of God and foresighted faith in this business of predestination; as if we were saying to elect from mere grace and good pleasure, and from foresighted faith; whereas the Apostle from the fact that the inheritance is of faith concludes that it is of grace, Rom. 4:16. But there is not a like reason of obtaining predestination or election, and of entering upon the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. In the business of election, to be of faith and to be of mere grace are ἐναντία (contraries), because this faith is presupposed to election, which is unto the first grace, and the fountain of all saving grace. But in the matter of entering upon eternal life they are not ἐναντία, because this faith is the gift of pure grace; and so the reward of life which is rendered to the believer is grace for grace. To this is added that since God has proposed to the human race a double way of obtaining salvation, one through the works of the Law, Do this, and you shall live; another through faith in the Mediator, Believe, and you shall be saved, it is rightly said that what is given from faith is given from grace; as what is given from the Law is from works. For it was the singular benefit of Gospel grace, the legal covenant being relaxed, to save sinners through faith. But on the other side the Remonstrants will never prove that God ordained a double mode of predestining men: one according to works, and another according to faith. If therefore some men were elected from an act of believing performed by them, and others were not elected because that same act was omitted, this discrimination would arise not from some special pact or act of Divine grace, but from discriminated acts of human wills. For Peter's predestination would be not from special grace of God, but from Peter's special work: because believing is here considered as a work of choice prevented by grace, opposite to the contrary act of disbelieving; not as a work of some Gospel covenant opposite to the Legal covenant, since concerning predestination such covenants do not exist on either side.
pass_b: Lastly Remonstrants say we err in opposing good pleasure (mere grace) to foresighted faith — as if electing from mere grace and from foresighted faith were rivals — since Paul, from inheritance being of faith, concludes it is of grace (Rom. 4:16). The cases are not alike. In election, of faith and of mere grace are ἐναντία: that faith is presupposed to election unto first grace, the spring of all saving grace. In entering eternal life they are not contraries: that faith is pure grace gift, so the life-reward rendered to the believer is grace for grace. God set the race a double path to salvation — Law: Do this and live; Mediator: Believe and be saved — so what comes by faith is rightly called grace, as what comes by Law is from works. Gospel grace singular gift, the legal covenant relaxed, is to save sinners by faith. Remonstrants will never prove God ordained a double mode of predestining — one by works, one by faith. If some were elected for a believing act they performed, and others passed over for omitting it, the split would come not from a special pact of divine grace but from differing human wills. Peter's predestination would then be from Peter's special work, not God's special grace: believing here counts as a work of grace-prevented choice against disbelieving — not as a Gospel-covenant work against the Legal, since no such covenants exist for predestination either way.

lemmas.gloss: inheritance of faith therefore of grace
